title: The backups looked fine. They'd been failing for three weeks.
metaDescription: A storage cap, a retention rule that could never fire, and three weeks of green checkmarks over dead backups — what it took to make silence itself an alarm.
tagline: A storage cap, a retention rule that structurally could never fire, and three weeks of green checkmarks over dead backups.
bullets: Every nightly run reported success — the off-site half hadn't uploaded in three weeks
Root cause: a retention rule that can never delete files that are never overwritten
The bucket filled to its storage cap and uploads quietly died
Now: the script prunes for itself, failures page a phone, and silence is an alarm

image.label: Timeline — cap exceeded → 23 silent nights → detection → paging

body: The server runs a nightly backup with two halves: a local snapshot, and an off-site bundle. The local half always succeeded. The off-site half had been failing since June 9 — and the job still exited clean every night, because an off-site failure was deliberately non-fatal (you don't want a cloud outage blocking a reboot). Reasonable decision, plus no one watching the warnings, equals three weeks of green.

It surfaced during a routine audit: the newest bundle in the bucket was 23 days old, and the error log said the same thing every night — storage cap exceeded. The bucket had a retention rule that looked exactly right: keep seven days, delete the rest. But that rule type only deletes prior versions of files that get overwritten or hidden, and every nightly bundle was a brand-new, unique filename that would never be either. The rule was perfectly configured to do nothing, forever.

sections.h: The fix was mostly not code
body: The code change was small: the script now prunes its own old bundles before each upload, and an immutability lock on the newest week means even a compromised server can't delete the copies that matter.

The bigger fix was making silence impossible. Warnings inside a 'successful' run now count, and a run with warnings sends one message to a phone. A separate check pages if backups simply stop happening. And a monthly restore drill is on the calendar — because a backup you've never restored is a hypothesis, not a backup.
Exit codes are claims, not facts — a job that exits 0 is asserting success, and something independent should be in a position to disagree.
Retention rules deserve the same testing as code: the question isn't 'is a policy configured' but 'has it ever actually deleted anything.'
And the failure mode that costs you isn't the loud one. It's the one that produces green checkmarks the whole time it's failing.
